items.title: Laid-off Stelco workers could be back on the job before Christmas, owner says
items.description: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.

items._ogDesc: Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves says he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.
items.body:
Cleveland-Cliffs Inc. CEO Lourenco Goncalves said Wednesday he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.

He said the company is now counting on increased purchases of Canadian-made steel, rather than tighter import restrictions, to restore jobs at its Ontario operations.

“It will depend on Canadian customers buying Canadian steel, made by Stelco,” Goncalves said in a statement to The Canadian Press. “If our plan works, my intention is to call back all the 175 workers before Christmas.”

In an internal letter to employees on Sept. 28, Stelco said up to 500 workers at its Hamilton Works and Lake Erie Works operations could be affected by layoffs. The steelmaker cited U.S. tariffs, weak demand for Canadian steel and competition from imported steel products as reasons for the layoffs.

But Goncalves clarified Wednesday that only 175 workers have been laid off.

Ron Wells, president of United Steelworkers Local 1005, which represents workers at Stelco’s Hamilton plant, confirmed that 175 workers have been laid off in Hamilton, while no layoffs have yet taken place at Lake Erie Works.

He accused Cleveland-Cliffs of using the layoffs to pressure Ottawa into tightening restrictions on foreign steel imports.

“He just caused a lot of pain and grief for 175 people,” Wells said. “Obviously, we’re against using our members as pawns.”

Industry Minister Mélanie Joly put Cleveland-Cliffs on notice last week to address alleged violations of its commitments under the Investment Canada Act, including employment guarantees, or face potential legal action. 

‘The clock is ticking’

In an emailed statement Wednesday responding to Goncalves’ proposed plan to recall workers, Joly reiterated that the company must provide a concrete plan and timeline for bringing employees back before she will agree to meet with him.

“We need a real plan from them to show us they are working in good faith,” she said. “The clock is ticking.”

The layoff announcement came roughly two years after Cleveland-Cliffs acquired Stelco in 2024. 

“We believed that we could sell cold rolled and galvanized steel within the Canadian domestic market, and that part did not materialize and has not improved yet,” Goncalves said in the statement. 

He said since Ottawa is unwilling to further restrict imports of cold-rolled and galvanized steel, Stelco will have to rely on its own efforts and Canadian customers to restore sales, production and jobs.

Goncalves also said Stelco will not be sold for at least the next year.

“I will not talk to any buyers, real or imaginary, now or within the next calendar year,” Goncalves said. “Conversely, after we demonstrate one year of higher production numbers, and also have brought all the 175 workers back to their jobs, I will be glad to sell the company, and only if I decide to do so by then.”

Joly has warned that Cleveland-Cliffs could be forced to sell Stelco if it fails to meet its binding commitments.

Goncalves said Joly is discouraging foreign investment in Canada by publicly discussing potential buyers for Stelco and criticizing the company’s business decisions.

“If I knew — or even suspected — that I would be subjected to this type of treatment when I made a business decision within the boundaries of undertakings that I am in full compliance (with), I certainly would not have invested in Canada,” he said.

‘We’re in contact with our lawyers’

Joly and Cleveland-Cliffs have also clashed over U.S. tariffs, which Goncalves has supported and Ottawa says have hurt Canadian steelworkers and contributed to the layoffs.

Joly told reporters Wednesday the federal government is consulting its lawyers about remarks by Goncalves suggesting he bought Stelco to protect his company’s U.S. operations from Canadian competition.

“We’re in contact with our lawyers ... to see what could be the consequences of such confessions,” she told reporters, referring to Goncalves’ comments during a televised interview.

Goncalves told CBC News on Tuesday that he bought Stelco because the Canadian company was flooding the U.S. market with steel and undercutting prices.

“I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company,” he told Power & Politics host David Cochrane.

The dispute also drew criticism from Liberal MPs on Parliament Hill on Wednesday, with Hamilton-area MP Lisa Hepfner accusing Cleveland-Cliffs of buying Stelco to undermine its Canadian operations and strengthen its U.S. business.

“They did not want that company to survive,” she said.

Liberal MP Yasir Naqvi, a former international trade lawyer, said Cleveland-Cliffs must honour its legally binding commitments regardless of its reasons for buying Stelco, calling them “ironclad obligations.”

The feud also reached Queen’s Park, where Ontario Economic Development Minister Vic Fedeli accused Cleveland-Cliffs of changing its story and supporting U.S. tariffs on Canadian steel.

“I think they’ve been disingenuous right from the very beginning,” Fedeli said. “They are on the team that has supported tariffs.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Brett Bundale, The Canadian Press

items.title: Alberta’s oil advantage comes with a costly catch as Bank of Canada raises interest rates
items.description: Alberta’s energy sector is benefiting from higher oil prices, but those same prices are contributing to inflation concerns that helped prompt the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates.

items._ogDesc: Alberta’s energy sector is benefiting from higher oil prices, but those same prices are contributing to inflation concerns that helped prompt the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates.
items.body:
CALGARY – Alberta’s energy sector is benefiting from higher oil prices, but those same prices are contributing to inflation concerns that helped prompt the Bank of Canada to raise interest rates Wednesday, adding to borrowing costs for Canadians already struggling with housing affordability.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

Calgary first-time home buyer Madeline Scarlett and her husband are hoping to find a permanent home for their young daughter after moving between rental properties.

“That would affect our monthly mortgage amount that we would pay,” Scarlett said of the rate hike. “That would affect our budget, like what we could afford.”

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5 per cent, its first increase since July 2023, with inflation at 3.1 per cent.

For Canadians with variable-rate mortgages, the increase could mean higher monthly payments.

In an email, Jordan Lavin, a financial expert with NerdWallet Canada, said variable mortgage rates are expected to increase as lenders adjust their prime rates.

“On a new $500,000 mortgage with a 25-year amortization, monthly payments at those rates would rise from $2,483 to $2,549 – a difference of $66,” Lavin said.

The calculation assumes lenders pass along the full quarter-point increase. Borrowers with fixed-rate mortgages would not see an immediate change to their existing interest rate.

The Bank of Canada’s decision comes as higher oil prices boost Alberta’s energy sector, but those same prices are also fuelling inflation concerns that helped prompt the rate hike.

The ongoing conflict in the Middle East has disrupted global oil supplies, driving up energy prices.

And while the industry is benefiting, Calgary realtor Sukh Pangly said not everyone is feeling the financial boost.

“I think there is a lot of job opportunity here in Alberta,” Pangly said. “That being said, just by having a job doesn’t necessarily mean you can afford that mortgage.”

He said Calgary’s housing market has shifted in buyers’ favour over the past six to seven months, with more listings, greater negotiating power and some builders offering incentives.

“You can get the GST rebate off the purchase price, builder incentives, getting legal basement suites to offset the mortgage, monthly payment,” he said.

But saving for a down payment remains a challenge for many households with other expenses to take care of.

“Juggle bills and inflation and daycare, gas, food, all that stuff,” Pangly said.

Economics professor Moshe Lander of Concordia University questions whether the Bank of Canada was justified in raising interest rates.

“One sector doing well does not necessitate an interest rate increase, especially when that one sector is not the overall driver of the Canadian economy,” Lander said.

He also questions the timing, pointing to uncertainty surrounding U.S. trade policy and global conflicts that could significantly change energy prices and the inflation outlook.

“I think this was maybe a little bit too early to make that move,” he said. “And I think that it’s going to do a lot more damage than it does good.”

For Scarlett, buying a home has already required financial assistance from others, including a co-signer.

“We can’t afford homes by ourselves anymore, unlike our parents back in the day,” she said.

Despite the challenges, Scarlett and her husband are continuing their search for a forever home.

With files from CTV News’ Judy Trinh

items._ogDesc: Discussions on the U.S. lifting sanctions on Russia’s flagship investment fund are underway with the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as saying on Wednesday.
items.body:
Discussions on the U.S. lifting sanctions on Russia’s flagship investment fund are underway with the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, Kremlin foreign policy aide Yuri Ushakov was quoted as saying on Wednesday.

Ushakov, quoted by Russian news agencies, said the head of the Russia Direct Investment Fund, Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev, was actively pursuing talks on lifting the sanctions.

“This conversation is going on. It has been going on for a while. I don’t know what the outcome will be,” Ushakov was quoted as saying.

“Dmitriev is active in his contacts and that’s why the issue is under discussion. It already got into the media a few days ago and discussions are still proceeding.”

The New York Times reported earlier in the day that the Trump administration was considering abandoning the sanctions.

Washington has made concessions to Moscow in terms of sanctions imposed following Russia’s February 2022 invasion of Ukraine.

Earlier this month, Trump announced that Russia would provide diesel for the U.S. and world markets, temporarily lifting sanctions on Russian fuel. Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak said on Tuesday that a fourth tanker of diesel would depart on Wednesday.

Trump also issued an executive order waiving key Russia-related U.S. sanctions and tariffs including duties on the country’s goods and penalties for buying its oil and gas, that had been scheduled to go into effect under the legislation known as the Graham Act that he signed into law last month.

items._ogDesc: A major firm is calling for Ottawa to remain impartial as it rolls out its nuclear strategy and the demand for clean energy soars.
items.body:
OTTAWA — A major firm is calling for Ottawa to remain impartial as it rolls out its nuclear strategy and the demand for clean energy soars.

Cameco CEO Tim Gitzel told a House of Commons committee on Wednesday that Ottawa needs to remain “technology neutral” in order to advance the country’s reputation and meet global market demand.

“Our competitors have the full support of their national governments. We don’t,” he said.

Canada launched a nuclear strategy in June that sets goals of doubling uranium exports and building up to 10 new nuclear reactors over the next 15 years.

The strategy also outlines a plan to boost foreign sales of Candu reactors, which are manufactured by Canadian company AtkinsRéalis, formerly SNC-Lavalin.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said earlier this month that AtkinsRéalis has a real shot at winning a lucrative tender to supply nuclear energy to Turkey — a prospect he said was remote a year ago.

Gitzel, whose company competes with AtkinsRéalis, said the federal government should “not put its finger on the scale” and advocate for all Canadian nuclear companies and their technologies.

Gitzel said Canada can be a “global nuclear superstar” but not if it limits technology diversification.

Gitzel argued the federal government was actively advocating against Cameco’s technology in markets like Poland where its nuclear reactors are under construction.

“It seems unfair to me that Canadian champions have to compete with their own government to be successful,” he told the committee. “Electrical utilities in Canada and around the world rely on Cameco to provide uranium, nuclear fuel and reactor technologies to generate nuclear power.

“Cameco is the nuclear fuel supply chain in Canada, and the reason Canada has a seat at the global nuclear fuel table.”

A spokesperson for Tim Hodgson, the minister of energy and natural resources, said the federal government has not endorsed one technology over another.

“Decisions about electricity generation fall within provincial and territorial jurisdiction, and provinces and our international partners are best placed to determine the technologies that meet their needs,” press secretary Charlotte Power said in a statement.

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

-With files from Nick Murray and Craig Lord

Catherine Morrison, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: Canadian Pacific Kansas City Ltd. is reporting flat profits despite a big boost in revenue in its latest quarter.
items.body:
The CEO of Canadian Pacific Kansas City Ltd. is calling out proponents of a massive proposed rail merger in the United States for alleged threats against customers.

Keith Creel said Wednesday that cautioning shippers against voicing resistance to Union Pacific’s attempted acquisition of Norfolk Southern would mark an attempt to “chill” dissent against a controversial marriage of two of the continent’s largest freight railways.

“My phone rings and people tell me when they get threatened. Customers share that,” Creel told analysts on a conference call.

“‘If you’re not for us you’re against us, don’t be on the wrong side of history ... don’t side with the losers,’” he said, citing warnings he claimed shippers have received.

  • Latest updates on company news here

The increasingly acrimonious battle over Union Pacific’s would-be US$85-billion acquisition of Norfolk Southern, announced in July 2025, is currently before American regulators.

Creel and other critics worry the deal could trigger a wave of mergers across an already concentrated sector — six companies dominate the North American rail industry.

Competitors and customers say the acquisition would cost shippers — and ultimately consumers — and place unprecedented market power in the hands of a single railway, which would handle some 40 per cent of American freight traffic.

Union Pacific and Norfolk Southern argue that getting hitched would slash costs and prompt rivals to lower their rates to compete.

On Wednesday, Creel pointed to an accusation levelled by U.S. Sen. Tammy Baldwin in a July letter to the U.S. Surface Transportation Board. She wrote that in a speech to a railway shippers association in Houston last March, Union Pacific chief executive Jim Vena made “a thinly veiled threat ... to raise rates for customers who did not publicly support the merger.”

Union Pacific has said the comment was “taken out of context” and suggestions to the contrary mark an effort to distract from the benefits of a transcontinental railroad.

In an email, the Chicago-based company said the acquisition is backed by more than 2,000 stakeholders, including more than 500 shippers.

Spokesperson Robynn Tysver said those customers “understand how this end-to-end combination will enhance competition and deliver broad public benefits” by shifting some two million truckloads from highway to rail transport, protecting union jobs and driving cost savings.

Despite his stated belief that merger approval is unlikely, Creel is steeling himself for the possibility. Should the deal get a thumbs-up, CPKC is asking regulators for safeguards to preserve competition, including gateway protections — so Union Pacific rivals cannot be barred from key interchanges — and shipper access to allow switching between railways.

“Not a Christmas list, a reality list,” he said, adding that the acquisition felt like a “lump of coal” in his view.

On Wednesday, CPKC reported flat profits despite a big boost in revenue in its latest quarter.

Net income attributable to shareholders stayed effectively flat at $917 million in the quarter ended Sept. 30 versus $920 million in the same period a year earlier, the Calgary-based railway said.

Third-quarter revenues rose 15 per cent year-over-year to $4.22 billion, bolstered by higher fuel surcharges but also a major jump in grain and shipping container volumes. The two categories saw revenues leap by 29 per cent and 22 per cent respectively, amounting to 42 per cent of freight revenues.

Coal, potash, fertilizer and automotive volumes all fell, but revenue rose across the board except for coal, where the cash intake was roughly on par with last year’s.

The company’s bottom line was dented by fuel costs that surged 61 per cent year-over-year to $667 million, making it the largest expense outside of labour due to the soaring price of diesel.

On an adjusted basis, core diluted earnings increased 16 per cent year-over-year to $1.28 per share from $1.10 per share, but fell short of analysts’ expectations of $1.32, according to financial markets firm LSEG Data & Analytics.

Christopher Reynolds, The Canadian Press

items._ogDesc: The head of the major projects office says Ottawa will need new ways to cut emissions to meet its climate goals because the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline will emit more than the Pathways carbon capture project.
items.body:
OTTAWA — The head of the major projects office says Ottawa will need new ways to cut emissions to meet its climate goals because the proposed Pacific Link oil pipeline will emit more than the Pathways carbon capture project will sequester.

Dawn Farrell, CEO of the major projects office, answered questions from MPs during an appearance before the House of Commons environment committee on Tuesday.

Citing the energy agreement between Canada and Alberta, Farrell told the committee the Pathways project is expected to reduce emissions by 16 million tonnes a year.

“We did assess what the greenhouse gas emissions would be from the pipeline itself, and it does bring up the emissions a bit,” she told the committee.

“And of course, Canada, through its various greenhouse gas strategies, will have to find a way to reduce that by 2050, given our goals for 2050.”

An analysis by Environment Canada, submitted to the committee and provided to The Canadian Press, projected the emission reductions from Pathways at 22 million tonnes a year.

Environment Canada also estimated that transporting an extra million barrels of oil a day through the new pipeline would increase emissions by 27.7 million tonnes.

To meet its 2030 target under the Paris Agreement, Canada still needs to reduce emissions by 227 million tonnes, according to the latest estimates from 2024.

One million tonnes is equivalent to what is emitted by 233,000 passenger vehicles over a year.

In July, Ottawa and Alberta signed an agreement with five of Canada’s major oil companies to advance the Pathways project.

The agreement made the Pacific Link pipeline conditional on getting Pathways built.

Asked by MPs on Wednesday what would happen if the oil companies suddenly reversed course and decided not to build it, Farrell said the major projects office could bake it into the conditions document for the pipeline.

“If Pathways wasn’t going to be underway, it would have to be a condition in our mind of the final conditions document that the Pathways project would be built in order for the (pipeline) to go ahead,” Farrell said.

“That’s what that conditions space is for.”

Manitoba Conservative MP Branden Leslie pressed Farrell over the fact that the conditions document issued by the major projects office is only a recommendation and the federal cabinet has the final say.

“Does cabinet have a veto on those conditions ultimately?” Leslie asked.

“You can make that as a recommendation. (But) can cabinet say, ‘No, in fact, never mind. We don’t need to build the pathways project. Go ahead with the pipeline’?”

“Well given that the Prime Minister is the one who’s very determined to have Pathways, I’m not sure why that would happen,” Farrell replied.

“But certainly cabinet, it’s at their discretion. They make the decision.”

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026

Nick Murray, The Canadian Press

With files from Lauren Krugel in Calgary

items._ogDesc: Some of Canada’s largest banks have moved to disallow third-party AI agents from accessing online banking.
items.body:
TORONTO — Some of Canada’s largest banks have moved to disallow third-party AI agents from accessing online banking.

RBC spokesperson Jeff Lanthier confirmed the move in a statement Wednesday, saying the bank has decided to block third-party personal AI agents from direct access to authenticated RBC digital properties, including online banking.

RBC CEO Dave McKay said in a post on LinkedIn on Tuesday evening that while the bank appreciates the benefits of AI being used to save time, “nothing is more important than the security of client information.”

  • Stay up to top of Canada’s biggest banks with BNN Bloomberg’s Big Banks Tracker

“If AI is going to move beyond the frontier and into the broader economy, trust will matter as much as capability,” the post reads.

BMO spokesperson John Fenton also said in a statement that it does not permit AI agents to access its digital properties or execute transactions in order to protect clients.

TD Bank has said it made the decision to block third-party personal AI agents, while CIBC said it does not support personal AI agents directly opening or accessing accounts.

National Bank said it is closely monitoring development of consumer AI agents. Scotiabank said it will limit third-party AI agents from its banking platforms while it monitors concerns.

items._ogDesc: Jury selection began on Wednesday in Los Angeles for another landmark trial about the alleged harms of social media on young users, with Meta and, for the first time, Snap as defendants.
items.body:
SAN FRANCISCO — Jury selection began on Wednesday in Los Angeles for another landmark trial about the alleged harms of social media on young users, with Meta and, for the first time, Snap as defendants.

Thousands of lawsuits have been filed in recent years in local, state and federal courtrooms across the country with various claims about alleged harms to children and teenagers caused by social media companies.

The cases -- the first of which went to trial earlier this year in Los Angeles -- have taken twists and turns.

Meta and YouTube lost the first so-called bellwether case earlier this year, when a jury found them collectively liable for harming a young user known by the initials KGM, and ordered the tech companies to pay a combined US$6 million penalty.

Meta said at the time that they “respectfully disagree” with the verdict.

Snap and TikTok settled with KGM ahead of that trial.

Months later, Snap, TikTok and YouTube settled another case that was set to go to trial in August; that plaintiff, known as RKC, then withdrew their remaining claims against Meta, allowing the Instagram and Facebook maker to avoid trial without a settlement.

TikTok and YouTube were previously named as defendants in the new case but both companies reached settlement agreements with the plaintiffs, known by their initials SJ and KDB, before the start of the trial, their lawyers said.

Meta reached a settlement agreement with one of the plaintiffs, SJ, but not KDB, according to their lawyers.

A California state judge consolidated both cases into a single trial.

If no additional settlements are reached before opening statements kick off on Nov. 4, the new trial will move forward with both Meta and Snap as defendants.

Star witnesses are expected to testify beginning mid-November including Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg, Instagram chief Adam Mosseri, and Snap CEO Evan Spiegel.

Earlier this month, a New Mexico judge ordered Meta to pay US25 billion in a case where the company was found liable for deceiving users in the state about how their data was used in a case related to the Cambridge Analytica scandal.

A New Mexico jury previously found the social media giant liable for harms to children, leading to a combined penalty of US$942 million.

In August, Meta agreed to pay more than US$18 billion in penalties, in addition to making changes to Instagram and Facebook for teens, when it settled with 52 attorneys general several days into a trial held in California.

Part of that settlement hinged on YouTube and TikTok making similar changes to their own products, such as limiting daily screentime.

‘Addictive and problematic’

As regulators around the world grapple with reining in, or even banning, social media use for teens, American lawsuits have focused on allegations of addictive design and deceptive practices by social media companies.

Next month, lawyers for the two plaintiffs in Los Angeles -- SJ and KDB -- will argue that their clients were exposed to “addictive and problematic” social media apps when they started using them at 13 and 15, respectively, according to court documents.

SJ, a teen in Illinois, began to use Snapchat, the app created by Snap, compulsively and subsequently experienced mental health issues, an eating disorder and self harm, her lawyers claim.

KDB, now an 18-year-old from Mississippi, similarly developed compulsive use of both Meta and Snap, leading to worsening mental and physical health, according to her lawyers.

“We disagree with these allegations and will defend ourselves in court,” Meta said in a statement.

Snap intends to argue that it is different from other apps like Meta’s Instagram and Facebook because of Snapchat’s focus on primarily being a messaging platform.

“We believe the evidence will support that we have put our community first, and that these allegations fundamentally misrepresent the plaintiffs’ experiences on Snapchat and how our platform was designed,” a Snap spokesperson said in a statement.

items.description: Foo Fighters’ 1997 hit “Everlong” has returned to the top of Billboard’s Hard Rock Streaming chart. Written by Dave Grohl during a difficult period in his life, the song continues to connect with listeners nearly three decades later.

items._ogDesc: Foo Fighters’ 1997 hit “Everlong” has returned to the top of Billboard’s Hard Rock Streaming chart. Written by Dave Grohl during a difficult period in his life, the song continues to connect with listeners nearly three decades later.
items.body:
Nearly three decades after it was written, Foo Fighters’ “Everlong” is proving that a rock song can outlast the era that produced it.

The 1997 hit has climbed back to No. 1 on Billboard’s Hard Rock Streaming chart for the week of Oct. 31, bringing renewed attention to one of the band’s most enduring songs.

Released as the second single from the group’s second studio album, The Colour and the Shape, “Everlong” has remained a fixture in Foo Fighters’ catalogue, connecting with longtime fans while continuing to reach new listeners.

  • How to set CTV News as your preferred source on Google

A song born during a difficult period

The track’s origins are closely tied to frontman Dave Grohl’s personal life. According to music publication Louder, Grohl began developing the song in late 1996 while staying at a friend’s home in Virginia during the breakdown of his marriage to Jennifer Youngblood.

What began as an acoustic guitar idea reportedly took about 45 minutes to put together. Grohl drew inspiration from his relationship with Louise Post, frontwoman of alternative rock band Veruca Salt, with the song capturing the intensity of romantic connection.

The track’s emotional themes, paired with its driving guitars and distinctive vocals, helped establish it as one of the defining songs in Foo Fighters’ catalogue.

A lasting legacy

Grohl initially had reservations about the song, reportedly wondering whether its sound resembled the work of Sonic Youth. He played a demo for the band’s Thurston Moore and Kim Gordon, who encouraged him to include it on the album, Louder reported.

That decision helped bring the song to a wider audience and cement its place in the band’s history.

items.title: The big question: How many more BoC rate hikes are ahead?
items.description: The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet
items.content: <p>The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639288097708752714.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The central bank delivered a 25-basis-point increase on Wednesday, and it may not be done yet
items.body:
The Bank of Canada delivered its first interest rate hike for over three years on Wednesday, sparking immediate questions about how far – and how fast – it might raise rates if it decides further increases are needed.

The central bank’s decision moved its benchmark rate to 2.5%, and its accompanying statement was frank that more hikes could be ahead if the inflation outlook worsens again.

For now, much will depend on the economic and inflation data that emerges in the months ahead, Bank of Montreal (BMO) managing director, Canadian rates and macro strategist Benjamin Reitzes told Canadian Mortgage Professional.

“It’s a little bit early to say how far they’ll go,” Reitzes said. “Looking at market pricing, there’s [a benchmark rate of] about 3.5% by the end of next year, a little further out. And that’s a bit on the aggressive side, I think.

“Getting that high suggests that you’d need a trade deal and some pretty good economic outcomes for that to come to fruition.”

At least one more hike seemingly ahead

It’s still safe to assume that the central bank will raise rates at least once more in the next several months, Reitzes said, either in December or January. The extent of the economy’s weakness in the coming weeks will be a crucial deciding factor in the timing of the next hike.

“The reason for their caution is that they have a pretty soft [GDP] forecast for the fourth quarter, just 0.8% growth,” he said. “If you have that amount of softness in the economy, do they really want to be hiking rates in that environment? The answer is probably no.

“They want to make sure that there is a rebound in growth. So if we do get some numbers coming over the next few weeks that point to a better fourth quarter, then that would be enough for them to likely [hike]. But we don’t get a lot of pieces of information between now and December, unfortunately.”

Central bank governor Tiff Macklem highlighted that persistent lack of clarity in remarks at the press conference following the announcement – a situation that’s exacerbated by ongoing geopolitical chaos.

“We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated,” he said. “Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid.”

Inflation concerns persist amid rising fuel costs

The annual inflation rate ticked higher in September, increasing to 3.1% amid continuing upward pressure on fuel prices caused by the US-Iran war.

Some economists viewed that as a mild enough reading for the BoC to keep rates steady in today’s announcement, but a growing number indicated a pre-emptive increase by the central bank was the likeliest outcome of its October decision.

Macklem said fuel costs would probably start to impact other types of inflation if they remain elevated. “The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly,” he said.

But the consumer price index (CPI) is still well below its 2022 level, when it ballooned to a 39-year high and prompted a flurry of big BoC rate hikes. The current environment, Reitzes said, is a “different world” to that era – mainly because of the weak growth outlook.

That means a steady stream of rate hikes by the central bank in the coming months remains unlikely for now.

“The likelihood of that resuming or something like that seems pretty low. We don’t have the level of stimulus globally that we had in the economy at that time,” he said. “You don’t have governments around the world pouring money into the economy and the post-pandemic surge in demand.

“We don’t have that type of event coming at this point. It’s more energy-price-driven. And we’ll see how the war in the Middle East goes. It’s just not the same backdrop – and the Bank just wants to make sure that they don’t let inflation take root again and have to deal with broader price pressures and then have to raise rates more aggressively later.”

items.title: BoC warns of 'subdued' outlook for housing market as rate hike raises borrowing costs
items.description: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.
items.body:
The Bank of Canada's rate hike Wednesday is set to translate to higher borrowing costs for homebuyers, adding further pressure as the real estate sector also copes with rising prices for construction materials.

The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, the first increase in more than three years, as it warned that inflation driven by the war in the Middle East is likely to spread.

"There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," the bank's senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers told reporters, as she described a "subdued" outlook for the sector.

"Certainly, borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin, so I think the outlook we've got for housing in the forecast here takes all of that into account."

The big question is whether the central bank's move is a one-time adjustment or the start of a sustained tightening cycle, said Phil Soper, president and CEO of real estate firm Royal LePage.

He said the sector's "prolonged weakness is already weighing on economic growth, and higher borrowing costs will only deepen that challenge."

Shawn Zigelstein, a broker for Royal LePage Signature Realty, said he believes the rate hike won't have a major effect on consumer confidence just yet.

"It's not like we are in a market like we were back in 2022 where the prices are increasing substantially on a regular basis," he said in an interview.

"A quarter-point adjustment really shouldn't make too much of a difference on someone's mortgage payments at this point."

The central bank's key policy rate had held steady for nearly a year following a series of cuts. Inflation ticked up to 3.1 per cent in September due to high gas prices, and the bank said an increase to the rate is necessary to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices spill over to other goods and services.

Zigelstein said clients he speaks with are more concerned about other day-to-day costs and whether the overall inflation environment makes it the right time to buy a home.

"They have been worried about other factors, including tariffs and such. Are they going to have the jobs that they had? Are their investments going to do what they've been doing? So they've got bigger concerns than worrying about interest rates," he said.

"Now, of course, if the rates start to change a little bit, then we will start to see potentially a little bit of a pullback on what people are spending because borrowing costs will be higher."

While Canada "is not facing a broad mortgage crisis," there are signs of financial pressure concentrated in specific regions such as the Greater Toronto and Hamilton Area and southwestern Ontario, said Aled ab Iorwerth, deputy chief economist for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corp., earlier this week.

He said trade tensions are weighing on key manufacturing sectors such as the automotive industry in those areas, leading to labour-market uncertainty and softer housing market conditions.

CMHC said Ontario's mortgage arrears rate reached 0.32 per cent in the second quarter, which is still below historical peaks but expected to continue rising through mid-2027. British Columbia and Atlantic Canada are expected to see a more moderate rise in mortgage arrears over the same period.

"The mortgage system is adjusting, but these early warning signs, particularly in parts of Ontario, need to be monitored closely," ab Iorwerth said in a news release.

Don Kottick, president of Re/Max Canada, said that while an interest-rate increase "may give some buyers pause," more balanced market conditions in many regions are creating opportunities for buyers, including greater choice and room to negotiate.

In September, the national average sale price fell 1.6 per cent year-over-year to $666,538, according to the Canadian Real Estate Association. National home sales were down 7.7 per cent from the same month last year, as the association cited higher fixed mortgage rates and the Bank of Canada's "notably more hawkish tone."

Fixed rates are largely unaffected by the Bank of Canada's decision, having already moved higher in recent months in line with the bond market. But further movement in the bond market into 2027 could prompt mortgage costs to jump, which "would have a dampening impact on home purchases," said Michael Waters, CEO of Minto Group, a real estate developer.

"Higher rates, everything else held equal, will reduce levels of purchaser activity for anything durable of size — cars and houses, certainly," Waters said in an interview.

"The housing sector is very slow right now and so that obviously would be a concern for anyone in that sector."

Meanwhile, the central bank said Wednesday that higher energy and import costs are expected to raise the costs of housing construction and maintenance through higher prices for materials and equipment.

Any increase to the cost of credit will also have an effect on the ability to build new projects, particularly new housing and supporting infrastructure, said Nicole Emmett, vice-president of communications, marketing and member services for the Canadian Construction Association.

"A home isn’t a home without the roads, sewers and watermains that support it, and higher borrowing costs put pressure on the margins of the contractors building them, which are already stretched by global supply chain disruptions and material costs," she said in a statement.

"Many contractors also rely on financing for equipment, materials and day-to-day operations."

Waters said higher interest — construction loans are based on a floating rate — along with rising input costs "will squeeze margins" and potentially lead to fewer large-scale project completions in the coming years.

"Certainly projects are far more challenged today than they would have been six months ago, pre-Iran war," he said.

"The impact would be fewer projects meeting economic feasibility tests and more projects probably sitting idle until market conditions improve, so that could have a negative impact on the creation of new housing supply."

This report by The Canadian Press was first published Oct. 28, 2026.

Sammy Hudes, The Canadian Press

items.title: Canadian household credit defies renewal shock, CIBC finds
items.description: Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture
items.content: <p>Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288083080510285.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Mortgage arrears keep rising, but CIBC economists see few cracks across the wider household credit picture
items.body:
Canadian borrowers are absorbing the mortgage renewal shock better than most forecasters expected.

Credit scores are improving and early-stage delinquencies are easing, even as more homeowners fall seriously behind on their mortgages.

That is the conclusion of a new report from CIBC Capital Markets economists Benjamin Tal and Katherine Judge, who revisited household credit quality a year into the mortgage payment cliff.

Their verdict came two days before the Bank of Canada raised its overnight rate to 2.5%.

“Simply put, the credit quality position of Canadian households is surprising on the upside,” they wrote.

Mortgage arrears remain the weak spot

The exception is the mortgage book itself. The share of mortgages 90 or more days in arrears keeps climbing and now sits well above its pre-pandemic level, as borrowers renew at higher rates into a softer labour market.

CIBC estimates that payment jumps of more than 40% hit 5% to 6% of all outstanding mortgages in 2026.

Regionally, the strain is uneven, with mortgage arrears in Ontario expected to keep worsening until mid-2027.

“I think [delinquencies] will continue to increase as more homeowners renew their mortgages in the next 12 months, 24 months even. But I think it’s going to be a slow grind,” Victor Tran, mortgage and real estate expert at Rates.ca, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year.

Still, serious delinquencies on credit cards and lines of credit held by mortgage borrowers have levelled off. Because most households stop paying those debts before missing a mortgage payment, CIBC treats them as an early warning, and that warning has gone quieter.

Derek Serra of Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation says the Canadian housing market is still feeling the effects of pandemic-era low interest rates, as borrowers face higher renewal costs and affordability challenges. https://t.co/Dcwt1JphsT — Canadian Mortgage Professional Magazine (@CMPmagazine) October 28, 2026

Proposals, not bankruptcies

Elsewhere, the numbers point to normalization rather than distress.

Household debt is growing at about 4%, near a record low outside the pandemic, and mortgage balances rose roughly 2% year over year in August, the weakest pace in 25 years. Average credit scores sit 1.3% above 2019 levels.

Insolvencies are up 6% over the year but are only now approaching 2019 levels.

Consumer proposals, which typically cost lenders less than bankruptcies, made up 77% of filings in the third quarter, compared with 60% in 2019. Equifax data on Canada’s insolvency hotspots suggests that choice is deliberate.

“A lot of the insolvency rates that we’re seeing an increase in is really tied to homeowners that want to protect their assets but obviously have a mountain of non-mortgage debt, and they’re trying to find a way to formally reduce that through more structured payments so that they can stay afloat,” Kathy Catsiliras, Equifax Canada’s vice-president of analytics and consulting, told CMP.

CIBC expects renewal payment increases to ease notably from February 2027, with mortgage delinquencies likely to trend lower that year, depending on the job market.

Until then, the Bank of Canada’s first rate hike since 2023 adds pressure where households are already stretched, according to Joel Fox, chief operating officer of Ownright.

“For most people, the 25 basis points on its own isn’t a dramatic change by any means. On a $500,000 mortgage, it’s roughly $60 to $70 more a month, depending on the amortization. The problem is that it can really affect households that have already been struggling,” Fox said.

“Plenty of people locked in at very low rates a few years ago, and they’re now renewing into a much bigger payment. This hike doesn’t help.”

His advice for borrowers nearing renewal: “If you’re renewing in the next year, start early. It’s a good idea to talk to your lender or broker, compare offers and know what your payment will be before the renewal notice shows up. Pick something you can live with instead of hoping and waiting for rates to fall.”

items.content: <p>The fintech secures fresh backing as its client base grows to 4 million Canadians</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/ca/046/0379_637595963905457520.jpg" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The fintech secures fresh backing as its client base grows to 4 million Canadians
items.body:
Wealthsimple Technologies Inc. has closed an equity round of up to CAD $425 million at a post-money valuation of CAD $13.8 billion. That's nearly 40% above the CAD $10 billion mark the Toronto-based financial technology company reached in October 2025.

GIC, the Singapore sovereign wealth fund that co-led last year’s fundraise, is again leading the round, alongside Power Corporation of Canada, IGM Financial Inc., ICONIQ, Canada Pension Plan Investment Board (CPP Investments) and Inovia.

The deal is structured as a CAD $300 million primary offering alongside a secondary component of up to CAD $125 million, an arrangement designed to let employees share in the value they have helped create.

“This raise reflects the deep conviction our partners have in Wealthsimple’s mission and in our role as the company defining the future of financial services in Canada,” said Michael Katchen, CEO and co-founder of Wealthsimple, in Toronto.

“These investors know our business deeply and chose to increase their commitment. With their support, we will keep building and innovating until every Canadian can live their entire financial life on Wealthsimple.”

Leaving the banks behind

As of September 30, Wealthsimple held CAD $169.2 billion in assets under administration, up 69% from CAD $100 billion at the time of its October 2025 fundraise.

The company now serves more than 4 million Canadians, including one in four aged 18 to 40.

In Q2 2026, new chequing account openings outpaced new investment accounts for the first time in the company’s history.

What it means for mortgage brokers

Wealthsimple’s growing product suite includes a Portfolio Line of Credit, allowing clients to borrow against their investment holdings, alongside a business chequing account, a prepaid Visa card and cash deposit access at more than 5,300 Canada Post locations across Canada.

In the past year, the company launched more than 50 new products spanning trading, chequing and business tools.

As Canadian mortgage industry observers track how fintechs are gaining ground in the mortgage market, the concern is as much about where clients park their savings and equity as it is about which lender wins the deal.

That shift has been closely followed by the sector. Naga Parvatharajan, chief executive of Ratehub.ca in Toronto, told Canadian Mortgage Professional earlier this year – while discussing how OSFI’s new approvals framework is opening the market to fintechs – that greater competition among financial institutions means Canadians gain “better rates and innovative options,” a dynamic that has historically served the broker channel well.

Tanya Woods, head of government and regulatory affairs and policy counsel at Questrade Financial Group, in Toronto, offered broader context to CMP when examining what open banking could mean for Canada’s mortgage market in the years ahead.

" The fact that Canadians might be able to see their entire financial picture on a single dashboard one day is very exciting because they will have a much greater sense of what they can afford and where the opportunities in their financial picture [are], so that they can make different or better decisions on housing," she said.

"Maybe they can afford more than they realized. Maybe they can find new ways to structure their debt because they get a better picture of the types of debt load that they’re carrying and where they can reduce it or leverage it positively. There’s so much opportunity."

items._ogDesc: The Bank of Canada raised rates to 2.5%, forecasting elevated inflation into 2028 as higher costs keep housing activity weak and push shelter inflation higher.
items.body:
Canada’s central bank raised its key policy rate as it tries to tame rising inflation. The Bank of Canada (BoC) hiked its overnight rate 25 basis points to 2.5% this morning, its first hike in over 3 years. In the accompanying report, the BoC warns of elevated inflation into mid-2028. Higher input and financing costs will also keep housing activity weak while boosting shelter inflation.

Canadian Inflation Isn’t Expected To Return To Target Until 2028

The BoC sees elevated inflation into 2028. The latest forecast from the central bank shows CPI inflation above 3% through Q3 2027. That’s roughly a point higher than they anticipated in their July report. It isn’t expected to return to their 2% target rate until mid-2028. While elevated inflation has largely been confined to energy and related categories, the Bank expects those pressures to spread over the next year.

High energy prices are spreading into production, transportation, and imports. Businesses have absorbed much of the increase so far, but expect to pass more on to consumers over the next 12 months, warns the BoC. Even after energy inflation turns negative in late 2027, earlier cost increases will continue to work their way through supply chains and boost prices.

Source: Bank of Canada.

Canadian Housing Investment Forecast To Lag The Economy

Higher rates are seen putting a drag on one of the country’s biggest components of GDP—housing investment. Residential investment primarily consists of spending on new home construction and substantial renovation. This sector is seen averaging less than 1% growth in 2027 and 2028. In contrast, GDP growth is expected to be roughly 2% for both years. The whole economy isn’t expected to slow, but housing will underperform.

Weak demand and high input costs are the reasons they cite. A lack of affordability, slow population growth, and rising borrowing costs are seen hitting the brakes on the demand side. Meanwhile, higher energy costs and imported input costs will make construction more expensive, throttling building activity.

Weak Housing Activity Isn’t Expected To Slow Rising Shelter Costs

Weak housing investment isn’t expected to slow shelter service inflation. It’s forecast to rise from just over 1% at the end of 2026 to 2% in 2027, and remain near that level into 2028. Higher material, equipment, construction, and maintenance costs are seen as the primary driver. Rising borrowing costs are expected to add further upward pressure. Rent inflation is seen as one of the few moderating factors for shelter, but it only partially offsets the other factors.

The impact on home prices isn’t clear, but higher expenses and weak demand aren’t bullish. At the same time, weak activity doesn’t automatically lead to affordability improvements.

The BoC report leaves an inflationary issue untouched: how government-backed construction spending supports higher input costs. Large projects compete for workers, resources, equipment, and land—even as private housing demand weakens. That spending can limit the disinflationary relief normally associated with a slowdown, leaving input costs elevated despite weak qualified demand.

items.title: Here's what Tiff Macklem said after the BoC's rate hike
items.description: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.content: <p>Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0388_639288017115537128.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Macklem warns oil price shock and Middle East conflict demand a policy response
items.body:
The Bank of Canada raised its policy interest rate by 25 basis points to 2.5% on October 28, its first increase since July 2023, as Governor Tiff Macklem declared the central bank's commitment to price stability in "this period of global upheaval," anchoring the decision in a Middle East oil shock and unsettled Canada-US trade relations.

Speaking alongside Senior Deputy Governor Carolyn Rogers in Ottawa, Macklem identified two developments that had shifted the Bank's calculus since July 2026: a deteriorating inflation outlook, with oil prices expected to "remain higher for longer" as the Middle East conflict persisted, and a stronger domestic recovery despite US tariff pressure.

"We are mindful that uncertainty is still elevated," he said.

"Developments in the Middle East and Canada-US trade relations both remain fluid."

Consumer Price Index (CPI) inflation has held near 3% since April and is projected to reach roughly 3.5% by year-end, with the 2% target not expected until mid-2028.

CPI excluding gasoline remains at 2.2% and core inflation sits near 2%.

"The longer energy prices remain high, the more likely it is these costs will spill over to consumer prices more broadly," Macklem said.

Oil, trade tensions, and the inflation risk that tipped the Bank's hand

Governing Council weighed that risk against solid economic data. Gross domestic product (GDP) grew 3.3% in the second quarter, with preliminary indicators pointing to about 2% growth in the third quarter, per the Bank of Canada's October 2026 Monetary Policy Report.

The unemployment rate has held near 6.5%, and full-year 2026 GDP growth is forecast at just 1% as US tariffs weigh on activity.

Not all forecasters agreed the moment called for action.Stéfane Marion, chief economist at National Bank of Canada (NBC) in Montréal, told the Mortgage Professionals Canada (MPC) conference in Calgary last week that core data argued for patience.

"Core inflation is still at 2%," he said.

"I don't think that the Bank of Canada should be hiking [on October 28] and if they do hike, they can't be too aggressive."

What the hike means for mortgage brokers

For Canadian mortgage brokers, the decision reshapes client conversations immediately.

Variable-rate mortgage holders will see payments rise as lenders' prime rates move from 4.45% to 4.70%, a shift that renewal discussions and rate-path strategy had been building toward all year, and Wednesday's announcement intensifies the pressure.

Leah Zlatkin, a Toronto-based licensed mortgage broker and expert commentator with LowestRates.ca, said one move is unlikely to be the last.

"If there is a hike, I do think it's going to be a cycle," Zlatkin said.

TD Bank economist Marc Ercolao, speaking from Toronto, said Macklem had telegraphed the outcome weeks earlier.

"It was Bank of Canada Governor Macklem's remarks a couple of weeks ago that likely tipped the scales towards today's decision to hike," Ercolao said.

"The Bank of Canada said it does not see a clear offramp to the conflict in the Middle East and is increasingly worried about the risks to inflation."

Governing Council signalled caution on what comes next, stopping short of any firm commitment to further action.

"Looking ahead, Governing Council agreed we would take future decisions one meeting at a time," Macklem said.

"There could be a need to raise the policy rate further, but given the uncertainties, we will proceed carefully."

The Bank's next rate decision is set on December 9.

items.title: Only 18% Of Young Canadians Fully Confident About Homebuying Finances: Survey
items.description:
Just 18% of Canadians aged 18 to 34 say they feel confident navigating all financial aspects of buying a home, according to the 2026 Zown Homeownership & Financial Confidence Survey, released Wednesday.

That compares with 35% of those aged 35 to 54 and 50% of those 55 and older.

Zown, an AI-powered real estate brokerage, conducted the survey from October 14 to 16 among 1,500 online adult Canadians who are members of the Angus Reid Forum.

The survey also found 40% of Canadians tapped into their long-term savings over the past year to cover expenses or unexpected costs.

Among those who did, 29% used the money for emergencies or unexpected expenses, and 22% for groceries and everyday purchases. Another 13% put it toward regular housing costs, including rent or mortgage payments.

Alberta had the highest share of respondents drawing on long-term savings, at 48%. Saskatchewan and Manitoba combined came in at 44%, followed by Ontario and British Columbia at 41% each, Atlantic Canada at 35%, and Quebec at 34%.

“Housing affordability isn’t just about the price of a home. It’s also about whether Canadians can afford to become homeowners in the first place,” said Rishard Rameez, founder and CEO of Zown.

“There’s a disconnect between the dream of homeownership and the financial reality many Canadians face. We’re asking people to save tens of thousands of dollars for a down payment when they’re already drawing on their savings to cover everyday expenses. That’s a fundamental challenge we can’t afford to overlook.”

For the younger group, saving and planning for a downpayment and understanding the ongoing costs after buying a home were the areas of least confidence, at 19% each. Knowing how much home they can afford came next at 18%, then knowing which homebuying incentives or programs they qualify for (14%) and understanding closing costs (10%).

Ownership makes a similar difference. Only 13% of Canadians who have never owned a home, but haven’t ruled it out, feel confident across every financial aspect of buying one, compared with 46% of current homeowners.

For those prospective buyers, the downpayment is the area of least confidence, cited by 30%. Understanding how much home they can afford follows at 18%, and the ongoing costs of homeownership at 14%.

items.title: AI tools may make women sound less sophisticated at work
items.description: A new study raises questions about how AI-generated writing could shape perceptions of professionalism and competence
items.content: <p>A new study raises questions about how AI-generated writing could shape perceptions of professionalism and competence</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/035/0394_639283811160256015.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: A new study raises questions about how AI-generated writing could shape perceptions of professionalism and competence
items.body:
Two people can ask an AI chatbot for the same workplace email and get noticeably different results, depending on little more than their choice of words.

That’s the finding at the center of new research from Johns Hopkins University in Baltimore. Researchers tested four widely used chatbots, GPT-4, Llama, Gemma and Mistral, with prompts for workplace emails, job applications and resignation letters.

When they rewrote the prompts to include language more commonly associated with women, such as hedges like “maybe” and “I think,” collective phrasing like “we” and “our team,” and expressive adjectives like “lovely” and “wonderful,” the responses came back less complex, at a lower grade level and less formal.

Katherine Van Koevering, an inaugural postdoctoral fellow at the university’s Data Science and AI Institute and the study’s lead author, said the size of the difference surprised the team.

“The headline finding, of course, is that when we rewrote prompts asking for workplace communication using more women-associated linguistic features, the model output was of a lower complexity level, lower grade level, I believe less formal,” Van Koevering said. “It looked surprisingly different.”

Anjalie Field, the study’s senior author and a Johns Hopkins computer scientist in Baltimore who studies ethics and discrimination in AI, said earlier research has examined bias in what the models produce.

“There’s been a lot less research that really focuses on the perspective of people using these models and how models perform for different groups of people or even different individuals,” Field said.

Ruling out mirroring

One obvious question is whether the models were simply echoing the style of the person writing the prompt. To test for that, the researchers measured the complexity of each prompt and compared it with the complexity of the response.

“We would measure the complexity of the prompt, and then we compare that to the complexity of the output,” Van Koevering said. “That would tell us how much of this is mirroring versus the AI picking up on something else.”

“Mirroring only accounted for, I think, a third or less, even at our highest level of mirroring,” she added.

In most cases the share was much smaller. At the highest level, mirroring explained about a third of the complexity differences, which generally isn’t enough to undermine the statistical significance of the findings.

The effect appeared in all four tools, though its strength varied by model.

“I wouldn’t say it was exactly the same, but the significance of the results held for every model we tested,” Van Koevering said.

What it could mean for workplace writing

With mirroring explaining only part of the difference, attention turns to what the results mean at work.

“Anyone who uses this kind of language, who uses things like hedges or expressive adjectives, could be getting outputs from models that are less sophisticated, less complex, and less formal,” Field said.

“If you prompt a model with this kind of language and you then take that output and send it to your colleague, that’s going to reflect on you and how they think about you,” she added.

The researchers also asked an AI to compare outputs from woman-associated and man-associated prompts and say which seemed more authoritative and competent.

“[The AI] chose the output for the male sociolinguistic feature prompts most of the time,” Van Koevering said.

She said there’s some suggestion that the effect extends beyond how sophisticated the writing sounds to how competent and authoritative it comes across.

Van Koevering said the pattern may extend well beyond gender, too.

“In theory, this works on any kind of linguistic differences,” she said. “If you type with British spelling, maybe it responds to you differently. If you use slang, maybe it responds to you differently.”

The team also tested whether including a traditionally male or female name changed the response. It had virtually no effect, according to the Johns Hopkins release.

Other research has looked at how AI systems treat gender in workplace settings. In a University of Washington study of AI resume screening that its authors summarized in an April 2025 Brookings Institution article, men’s and women’s names were selected at equal rates in only 37% of 27 resume screening tests across three language models and nine occupations. HRD America has also reported on University of Chicago research showing that women were less likely than men to use ChatGPT in the same occupation, and on an International Labour Organization warning that generative AI could affect women’s jobs more than men’s.

What companies and workers can do

Asked what organizations should do with the new findings, Field said flagging the issue to staff is one option.

That would mean providing guidance that many workers say they haven’t received. In a May 2026 survey of 1,020 employees by career platform Resume Now, 41% said their employer has given them no tools, training or guidance for using AI, HRD America reported.

For individual workers, Field said one way to handle it is to be careful about how they prompt a model and to check that the style and tone of the output match what they want to send. She said adding instructions about the desired tone to a prompt is another option, though the team didn’t explicitly test it.

Van Koevering said workers can test the effect themselves.

“Write it how you would imagine writing it, and then make up some personas in your head and write it different ways and just see the difference,” she said.

She said the drawback is the extra time it takes to rework writing people have probably already spent a lot of time on.

Field said she doesn’t like these workarounds as a long-term solution because they put the burden on the user. In her view, the models should be trained to pay attention to the tone and style each type of request calls for, however it’s phrased.

“That’s not a solution for HR managers. That’s what the technologists should be working on,” Field said.

In the meantime, the researchers’ suggestions come down to awareness and testing. Employers can make sure staff know that the way a request is phrased may change the tone of what an AI tool writes, and workers can check that tone before a message goes out.

Until the models themselves change, the findings suggest the same request can still come back sounding different depending on how it’s worded.

items.title: Bank Of Canada Raises Policy Rate To 2.5% In First Hike Since 2023
items.description:
The Bank of Canada raised its target for the overnight rate by 25 basis points on Wednesday, bringing it to 2.5% and marking the first increase since July 0f 2023.

The Bank Rate now sits at 2.75%, and the deposit rate at 2.45%.

Inflation is running higher and longer than the Bank projected in July. CPI inflation has hovered around 3% since April, and the Bank expects it to climb to about 3.5% by the end of the year, largely because of persistently high oil prices.

Take gasoline out and the numbers look calmer. Inflation excluding gas was 2.2% in September, and core measures remain close to 2%. The Bank is more worried about where costs are heading. High fuel prices are raising production and transportation costs, imported industrial and electronics inputs have become more expensive, and Bank surveys suggest businesses will pass more of those costs on to customers over the next year.

The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month with no clear path to resolution. The Bank expects CPI inflation to average 3% in 2027, a full percentage point above its July projection, before easing to 2% in the middle of 2028.

Governing Council said the hike is meant to reduce the risk that high energy prices spread into the prices of other goods and services. It said further increases may be needed, but that it would proceed carefully given the uncertainty.

The economy has outperformed expectations. GDP grew 3.3% in the second quarter, and recent indicators point to about 2% growth in the third, both stronger than the Bank anticipated. Consumer spending held up despite slow population growth, and business investment rebounded on oil and gas activity and machinery and equipment spending. Unemployment has held around 6.5% for several months.

New US tariffs are expected to slow growth in the fourth quarter. The Bank projects the economy will grow 1% in 2026 and 2% in both 2027 and 2028, a somewhat stronger outlook than July’s, though Canada-US trade relations remain a major source of uncertainty.

Business investment, exports and fiscal measures are expected to drive the 2027 rebound. Housing, however, isn’t on that list. The Bank expects it to remain relatively weak, with consumption growth moderating as well.

items.title: BoC hikes rates for the first time in over three years
items.description: Central bank moves rates higher as inflation fears rise
items.content: <p>Central bank moves rates higher as inflation fears rise</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287915827940101.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: Central bank moves rates higher as inflation fears rise
items.body:
The Bank of Canada has hiked its benchmark rate for the first time since July 2023 amid rising fears about the national inflation outlook.

The central bank said on Wednesday morning it was raising that trendsetting interest rate by 25 basis points to a level of 2.50%, ending its long wait-and-see approach on the rate question.

Major Canadian lenders are expected to increase their prime rates following the decision. Variable mortgage rates, as well as home equity lines of credit (HELOCs), typically rise and fall in tandem with Bank of Canada moves.

Odds of a rate jump by the BoC had risen in recent weeks as fuel costs continue to surge, mainly because of the ongoing US-Iran war.

The overall consumer price index (CPI) climbed only modestly month over month in September (to 3.1%, up by 0.1%), but the Bank’s move will be viewed as a pre-emptive bid to stave off the threat of higher energy costs spilling into other sectors.

The hike is the Bank’s first step off the sidelines in 2026. It’s held rates steady through the year to date as it weighs a sluggish national economy against growing concerns on the inflation front.

While the Bank kept rate hikes on ice until today, fixed mortgage rates rose steadily in September because of the upward trajectory of five-year Government of Canada bond yields.  

BoC governor Tiff Macklem will face the media at about 10:30 a.m. ET this morning and could give some indication of whether further rate hikes are likely in the months ahead.

What’s next for the BoC?

For now, it looks unlikely that the central bank will embark on a series of steep hikes similar to the last time it started raising rates.

In March 2022, the BoC bumped rates 25 basis points higher after nearly two years at rock-bottom lows of 0.25% – and that was a sign of things to come, with its policy rate spiking by a further 450 basis points in the 16 months following that move.

This time around, the weakness of the Canadian economy and the continuing negative impact of trade tensions with the US mean lenders and financial markets are pricing in only mild further increases by the Bank.

What the decision means for the housing market

For the housing market, it remains to be seen whether today’s decision will push potential homebuyers onto the sidelines.

Housing and mortgage market watchers had been increasingly anticipating some rate increase by the BoC in recent weeks – but even the expectation of hikes hadn’t compelled many would-be buyers to rush into the market to secure mortgage rates at their current level.

The Bank has one further rate decision in store for 2026, with that announcement set for December 9.

items.title: Mortgage market ‘still recovering’ from BoC’s COVID rate cuts, says lender president
items.description: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.content: <p>The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive</p><img src="https://cdn-res.keymedia.com/cms/images/us/074/0373_639287200172090755.png" alt="" style="max-width:240px" />
items._ogDesc: The mortgage industry could be facing a much different environment if the central bank hadn’t decided to slash rates to record lows in 2020, says MIC executive
items.body:
The Bank of Canada is gearing up for what many pundits say could be the start of a new rate-hiking cycle – but the housing and mortgage markets are still dealing with the impact of its COVID-era rate policy even years later, according to the president of a prominent mortgage lender.

The central bank slashed its benchmark rate to a rock-bottom 0.25% at the onset of the pandemic, helping cause a homebuying frenzy as mortgage rates plunged and borrowers jumped into the market.

A series of rapid rate hikes in 2022 and 2023 put a halt to that housing boom, but Westboro Mortgage Investment Corporation president Derek Serra (pictured top) told Canadian Mortgage Professional he still sees the negative effects of the low-rate era seeping through.

“I think that we’re still kind of recovering from the decision to have lowered interest rates during COVID. And the outcome of that decision sparked such an incredible inflationary time for Canadians,” he said. “I’ve been in banking for 30 years, and I’ve always seen Canadians using the equity in their home as an opportunity for them to pay for their kids’ education.

“There was almost a kind of a familiarity or a consistency with expecting a little bit of growth in the value of your home. And so when these inflationary times came through COVID, which was triggered by the very low interest rates, the average Canadian saw rapid increases in their property values – which at the time sparked them to do more than what they usually do without, necessarily, the kind of long-term perspective.”

‘There was the opinion that rates… would stay low for a long time’

In 2025 and 2026, scores of mortgages originated during the pandemic have come up for renewal, almost always at much higher rates compared with five years prior.

That trend is part of the reason mortgage delinquencies are climbing, with Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation (CMHC) indicating on Tuesday it doesn’t expect the rise of mortgage arrears in Ontario to end until the middle of next year.

Serra suggested the Bank of Canada’s decision to dramatically cut rates in 2020 might have been the wrong one looking back.

“There was also kind of the opinion that rates would be low and stay low for a long time, and obviously that shifted for a variety of reasons,” he said. “And now we’re seeing the outcome of that decision.

“In hindsight, it’s always easy to look back and question, but you wonder if maybe we hadn’t dropped rates at the time, we would have felt more pain then – but it would have been a different kind of 2026 now.”

As the central bank embarked on a rate-hiking spree in 2022 and 2023, industry and expert opinion was divided on whether governor Tiff Macklem had misled Canadians by suggesting that interest rates wouldn’t be rising anytime soon.

Macklem told the House of Commons standing committee on finance in November 2020 that Canadians “can be confident that borrowing costs are going to remain very low for a very long time” – but within less than three years, the BoC’s benchmark rate had shot up by 475 basis points.

Critics said that reassurance may have convinced Canadians the time was right to purchase a home without factoring in higher costs down the line. Macklem’s defenders, on the other hand, pointed to unexpected developments including Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and the further supply chain snarls caused by the emergence of the Omicron COVID variant.

Appraisal challenges continue in higher-rate environment

As well as causing challenges for borrowers at renewal time, the post-pandemic march toward higher rates poured cold water on a red-hot housing market. In that environment, appraisal challenges have arisen because there are so few transactions in many cities to judge whether or how far a property’s value may have fallen.

Serra, though, pointed to some recent cause for optimism on that front. “The good news is we’ve seen a little bit of increase in the past four weeks in purchase transactions, and that is a really good sign,” he said.

“It’s an early indicator… but as we see purchase transactions, even if they’re at lower values, we’re able to now properly assess where the market’s at. If you’re living in a community where there haven’t been any sales, it’s very difficult to substantiate the value of these properties, especially for clients who are looking for higher loan-to-values.”
